newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIAN PRESIDENT TO GIVE TURKISH TIES NEW BOOST.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIAN PRESIDENT TO GIVE TURKISH TIES NEW BOOST.

text.p: Bulgarian President Petar Stoyanov leaves for Turkey on Monday, hoping to give a new boost to warming relations between the one-time Cold War foes.

Ties between the small Orthodox state of 8.4 million people and its bigger Moslem neighbour are burdened by five centuries of Ottoman rule in Bulgaria and by the forcible assimilation of Bulgarian ethnic Turks in the 1980s.

Stoyanov said he would ask his Turkish counterpart Suleyman Demirel to initiate Bulgaria's removal from an Organisation of the Islamic Conference (OIC) list of countries which do not respect Moslems' rights.

More than one million ethnic Turks were forced to give up their Islamic names and religious traditions under former communist dictator Todor Zhivkov, leading to an exodus of more than 300,000 to Turkey in 1989.
Their religious and cultural rights were restored after Zhivkov's overthrow in November 1989 and many of those who left have returned.

Zhivkov, 85, is under house arrest on charges connected to his assimilation policies, while the ethnic Turks' Movement for Rights and Freedoms, in coalition with monarchist parties, forms the third force in parliament.
"I will ask President Demirel to press for an OIC contact group to prepare a report on Moslems in Bulgaria ahead of December's OIC conference in Kuwait," Stoyanov said.
Under OIC statutes, it is Turkey which must initiate Bulgaria's removal from the list as it was Turkey which sought its inclusion in 1989.
Relations entered a new era after the collapse of communist rule. In May 1992 the Balkan neighbours signed a friendship and cooperation pact ending their Cold War enmity.
NATO member Turkey supported Bulgaria's application to join the alliance at this month's Madrid summit, though Bulgaria was not among the countries to join in the first wave of expansion.
"We might had have difficult times in the past, but now our joint efforts and friendly relations can only ease both countries' path to the European Union," Stoyanov said.
"Fate has chosen Bulgaria and Turkey to be neighbours, now it is up to us to choose to live in peace and understanding."
On his visit, postponed from mid-June to await formation of a new government in Ankara, Stoyanov will sign cooperation accords on defence, tourism, ecology and nuclear safety.

He will also propose a free trade agreement between the two countries and will discuss a regional initiative to combat organised crime and drug trafficking through the so-called Balkan route from Turkey via Bulgaria to Western Europe.
Stoyanov already raised the issue with Romanian President Emil Constantinescu, who visited Bulgaria in April.
Sources at the presidency said Stoyanov was expected to propose a trilateral meeting between the presidents of Bulgaria, Turkey and Romania, possibly in September.
